questions.q: What does qs.creation_time in sys.dm_exec_query_stats reveal?
options: The total number of rows the procedure has ever returned
The name of the login that created the stored procedure
Exactly when the cached plan was compiled, useful for correlating against other events like a statistics update
The physical fragmentation level of the underlying table
questions.explain: creation_time shows when the plan was compiled, letting you correlate it with the overnight statistics update and recompile.

questions.q: What does the controlled test in Step 2 prove?
options: Every provider is equally slow no matter what
Changing which @ProviderID compiles the plan first flips which provider is fast and which is slow
The stored procedure's T-SQL text was secretly edited
sp_recompile permanently disables the procedure
questions.explain: Forcing a recompile and running the typical provider first reverses the fast/slow pattern, confirming the plan — not the code — is the variable.

options: A feature that automatically creates a new plan for every single call
A method for detecting SQL injection attempts
A security vulnerability where parameters are exposed in plain text
A cached plan optimized for the first parameter value it compiled with, reused for all later, differently-shaped calls
questions.explain: SQL Server compiles one plan per procedure, optimized for whichever parameter value first triggered compilation, and reuses it regardless of fit for later calls.

questions.q: Why was the part-time provider's plan a poor fit for typical providers?
options: The plan was never actually cached in the first place
Typical providers don't have any rows in dbo.Appointments at all
The optimizer chose a seek-based plan suited to a handful of rows, which performs poorly against hundreds of rows
The part-time provider's plan contained a syntax error
questions.explain: A plan optimized for very few rows (Nested Loops/seek) is a poor fit for a provider with hundreds of appointments.

questions.q: Why didn't "no code change" rule this cause out, as Lesson 13 anticipated?
options: The plan changed (via recompile and a new sniffed parameter) while the procedure's own text never did
The code actually was changed, contradicting the original report
This bug only occurs after a schema change
Parameter sniffing requires a code change by definition
questions.explain: The stored procedure's T-SQL never changed — only which cached plan was in effect changed, which is exactly the parameter sniffing mechanism.
